market.name: Market signals
market.blurb: Every company in the scan with a material security signal, ranked. Narrow it with ICP filters, or start from a signal template.

templates.name: Newly exposed
templates.blurb: A risky service that was not in the previous scan: the clearest reason to call this week.
templates.pitch: It appeared since the last scan, and most incidents start with a change like this.

templates.name: Top priority (P1)
templates.blurb: The 500 highest-priority accounts across every signal: this week’s call list.
templates.pitch: Lead with the strongest finding on the account; the evidence panel orders it for you.

templates.name: Firewall/VPN with exploited CVEs
templates.blurb: An exposed firewall or VPN appliance plus CISA known-exploited CVEs in the same estate: the classic ransomware entry path.
templates.pitch: Edge devices are the most common way ransomware gets in, and this estate already runs software attackers are exploiting.

templates.name: Exposed firewall/VPN appliances
templates.blurb: FortiGate, NetScaler, SonicWall, Ivanti/Pulse or BIG-IP appliances answering on the internet: recognised by their own fingerprint, login or admin page, not by a certificate or header alone.
templates.pitch: Their firewall or VPN appliance answers on the public internet, the most common way ransomware gets in; keeping it patched and locking down its admin access is work you can do with them.

templates.name: On-prem Exchange
templates.blurb: Self-hosted Exchange or Outlook Web App on the internet: a ProxyShell-class attack surface.
templates.pitch: On-prem Exchange is one of the most attacked products there is; it opens an email-security or cloud-email conversation.

templates.name: Open RDP, databases & shares
templates.blurb: Remote access (RDP, WinRM), databases or Windows file sharing reachable from the internet.
templates.pitch: Anyone on the internet can reach their remote desktop or database today.

templates.name: Signs of a breach
templates.blurb: A ransomed database, a defaced site, a remote-access trojan or a cryptominer on the company's own address: it has already been breached.
templates.pitch: This is an incident, not a risk: offer an assessment and response this week, starting from the service it was found on.

templates.name: Exposed AI & MCP servers
templates.blurb: Self-hosted AI apps (LiteLLM, Ollama, Dify, Flowise) or MCP servers answering on the public internet, often without a login.
templates.pitch: Their AI tooling is reachable by anyone; an exposed model gateway or agent server can leak keys, data and tool access.

templates.name: Legacy Windows estates
templates.blurb: End-of-life Windows Server, or NTLM banners leaking the internal Active Directory domain.
templates.pitch: Unsupported Windows Server no longer gets security patches, and their servers reveal the internal domain to anyone.

templates.name: Known-exploited CVEs
templates.blurb: Software on a version affected by a CVE on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list: verified by the scanner, or a versioned product that isn’t a distro package patched in place.
templates.pitch: They run software with vulnerabilities that attackers are exploiting right now, per CISA.

templates.name: OT & IoT exposure
templates.blurb: Industrial, medical or point-of-sale protocols and cameras on the internet.
templates.pitch: Operational equipment is reachable from the internet; a compliance-led conversation (IEC 62443, NIS2).

templates.name: Already investing
templates.blurb: Has a WAF, security.txt or post-quantum TLS but still has gaps.
templates.pitch: They already buy security; talk coverage gaps and consolidation, not a first purchase.
